stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: A flat transmission spectrum, one showing no absorption features, was long read as evidence that an exoplanet lacks an atmosphere. Astronomers now recognize that a high-altitude aerosol layer, such as photochemical haze or silicate cloud, can produce the same flat spectrum by blocking starlight before it reaches the gases below. Photochemical hazes are thought to form only on planets cooler than about 850 K, while silicate clouds are thought to condense only on planets hotter than about 1,300 K. The planet Veyra-4b has a flat spectrum and a temperature of about 1,050 K, so ______
choices: its flat spectrum is better explained by silicate clouds than by the photochemical hazes found on cooler planets.
it must lack an atmosphere, since both kinds of aerosol layer have been excluded as causes of its flat spectrum.
neither of the two aerosol layers described is a likely source of the flatness in its spectrum.
planets with temperatures between 850 K and 1,300 K are less likely than other planets to retain atmospheres.
explanation: You need three facts at once. At 1,050 K, Veyra-4b is above haze's ceiling of 850 K, so haze is unlikely. It is also below the 1,300 K floor for silicate clouds, so those are unlikely too. Put together, neither named layer accounts for the flat spectrum. That is as far as the chain goes. Haze and silicate cloud are given only as examples ('such as'), and the temperature limits are only 'thought' to hold. So the passage supports ruling out these two layers. It does not support any conclusion beyond that.

A.why: You used only half the chain. You saw that 1,050 K is too hot for haze and stopped there, so you never checked the silicate-cloud threshold. Those clouds condense only above 1,300 K, so the planet is too cool for them as well.

B.why: You got the key point that both layers are ruled out, then took one extra step. The passage gives haze and silicate cloud only as examples ('such as'), so other aerosols aren't excluded. The thresholds are also only 'thought' to hold, so 'must' claims more certainty than the passage gives.

D.why: You went from one planet to a claim about a whole temperature range. The passage says nothing about how often planets in that range keep their atmospheres. It doesn't even establish that Veyra-4b has lost its own.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Traffic-safety campaigns usually judge a street by how often collisions occur on it. A study of twelve residential streets in the city of Ardell, however, found that cutting the speed limit from 30 to 20 miles per hour left the number of collisions essentially unchanged while sharply reducing the share that caused serious injuries. Separately, city hospital records show that collisions causing serious injuries account for most of the traffic-related admissions to Ardell's trauma wards. Taken together, these findings suggest that lower speed limits on residential streets ______
choices: would reduce trauma-ward admissions chiefly by making collisions on those streets less frequent.
could reduce traffic-related trauma-ward admissions even without making collisions any less frequent.
would cut Ardell's traffic-related trauma-ward admissions by more than half within a few years.
would lower trauma-ward admissions more than any other safety measure Ardell has tried.
explanation: The term the two facts share is serious-injury collisions. The total number of collisions stayed the same while the share that were serious fell, so the number of serious-injury collisions fell. Those collisions cause most traffic-related trauma admissions. Chaining the two facts, lower limits could reduce those admissions even though collisions are no less frequent. 'Could' fits the passage's 'suggest'. The choice also keeps the part of the finding that held steady: the number of collisions didn't change.

A.why: You linked lower speed limits to fewer admissions but credited the wrong half of the split finding. The study says the number of collisions was essentially unchanged. Only how severe they were changed.

C.why: You combined 'most' and 'sharply' into a specific figure. The passage gives no amount for either, no timeline and no citywide results; the study covered only twelve streets. 'Suggest' supports only a possible reduction, not a measured one.

D.why: You went past the chain to a comparison no one made. The passage never mentions any other safety measure, so it can't support a ranking.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many folklorists assume that the longer a tale has circulated, the more versions of it collectors will find. Folklorist Ilse Hartmann challenges this view. In her survey of Baltic archives, a tale's number of recorded variants tracked the number of distinct dialect regions it had crossed, not its age. She also found that tales told mainly at seasonal markets had crossed more dialect regions than tales told mainly within households. Taken together, Hartmann's findings suggest that ______
choices: tales told mainly at seasonal markets have generally circulated for longer than tales told mainly within households.
a household tale would likely have fewer recorded variants than a market tale that has circulated for a similar length of time.
every tale told mainly at seasonal markets has more recorded variants than any tale told mainly within households.
household tales gather variants more quickly than market tales do, because families retell them more often.
explanation: The shared term is dialect regions. Variants track dialect regions crossed, and market tales cross more regions than household tales. Remove the middle term and you get this: market tales tend to have more variants than household tales. Because Hartmann found that age does not drive the count, the comparison holds even when the two tales are the same age. The word 'likely' matches the 'suggest' in the passage.

A.why: You added a claim about age that the passage never makes. Hartmann's point is that age is not what drives the variant count, so nothing here tells you which kind of tale is older.

C.why: You linked the two facts correctly but then made the link absolute. A tendency across a survey does not mean every market tale beats every household tale. 'Every' and 'any' are claims nobody established.

D.why: You fell back on the popular view the passage undercuts. The evidence points to market tales having more variants, not household tales, and the passage says nothing about how often families retell their tales.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In a twelve-week study, sprinters who trained on sand developed stiffer ankles, while their stride length did not change. Earlier research had established two things. Greater ankle stiffness shortens the time a sprinter's foot spends on the ground. And shorter ground contact raises top speed only for athletes whose stride already exceeds 2.1 meters. For a sprinter in the study whose stride measured 1.9 meters before training, the researchers would therefore predict that sand training ______
choices: shortened the sprinter's ground contact and, as a result, raised the sprinter's top speed.
shortened the sprinter's ground contact but did not raise the sprinter's top speed.
lengthened the sprinter's stride past 2.1 meters, letting shorter ground contact raise top speed.
raised the sprinter's top speed while leaving the sprinter's ground contact unchanged.
explanation: Follow the chain. Sand training increases ankle stiffness, and stiffer ankles shorten ground contact, so ground contact gets shorter. Shorter contact raises speed only when stride is above 2.1 m. Stride did not change, so this sprinter is still at 1.9 m, below the cutoff. No rise in top speed is predicted.

A.why: You saw the first link and finished the chain the obvious way. You skipped the 'only for' condition. With a 1.9 m stride, shorter contact is not linked to higher speed.

C.why: You assumed stride changed. The passage says stride length did not change with sand training, so the sprinter stays below 2.1 m.

D.why: You reversed which variable moved. Stiffer ankles are what shorten ground contact, so contact should change. Speed is the one with no predicted gain.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: It is often said that Baroque composers chose keys for their emotional character. Musicologist Adaeze Oyelaran argues that for works with natural horns, practicality decided. A natural horn could play only the notes of one key's harmonic series, and that key was set by a detachable tube called a crook. Oyelaran also notes that the court orchestra at Weissenfels owned crooks only for D and F. Taken together, these points imply that a horn part in a work for the Weissenfels orchestra ______
choices: would have been set in D or F because those keys conveyed the mood the composer wanted.
could have been written in any key, provided a suitable crook was fitted to the horn.
would have been confined to the notes of the harmonic series of D or of F.
belonged to a work that was itself in D or F, as was every piece the court performed.
explanation: The term the two facts share is the crook. A crook fixes the horn to one key's harmonic series, and Weissenfels had crooks only for D and F. Remove the middle term and a Weissenfels horn part is limited to the D or F harmonic series. That is all the two facts establish together.

A.why: You reached the right keys but gave the reason the passage undercuts. Oyelaran says practicality decided the key, not emotional character.

B.why: You used only the first fact, that crooks set the key, and ignored the inventory. Weissenfels had crooks only for D and F, so 'any key' was not available.

D.why: You stretched a limit on horn parts into a claim about every piece the court performed. Nothing in the passage limits works without horns.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Historians once dated medieval tapestries by their dyes. But madder and weld were in use for centuries, so a dye can place a tapestry only within a very wide span. Textile historian Mareike Kessler dates them by the twist of the warp thread instead. She has shown that Flemish spinners switched from S-twist to Z-twist warp around 1420, and that Arras workshops adopted each Flemish spinning change within a decade of its appearance. A tapestry woven in Arras with S-twist warp was therefore most likely made ______
choices: no later than about 1420.
no later than about 1430.
between about 1420 and 1430.
sometime after about 1430.
explanation: Link the two facts. Flanders switched to Z-twist around 1420, and Arras followed within ten years, so Arras had switched by about 1430. An Arras piece that still uses S-twist must therefore come from before that point. Nothing more precise follows: it could be from 1425 or from 1380.

A.why: You used only the Flemish date and forgot the Arras lag. An Arras workshop could still use S-twist for up to a decade after 1420, so a date of 1425 fits.

C.why: You found the right upper limit and then invented a lower one. S-twist was in use well before 1420, so nothing places the tapestry after that year.

D.why: You reversed the chain. After about 1430 Arras would be using Z-twist, so an S-twist warp points to a date before then, not after.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some researchers have proposed that *Clostridium* strain K7, a gut bacterium, protects mice from food allergy by acting on immune cells directly. Lin and colleagues found that colonized mice had more butyrate, a fatty acid the bacterium releases, and that butyrate expanded regulatory T cells, which suppress allergic inflammation. Butyrate given alone reduced allergy as much as colonization did, but it had no effect in mice lacking regulatory T cells. These results suggest that K7's protective effect ______
choices: depends on regulatory T cells only because K7 binds to those cells directly.
comes from butyrate calming allergic inflammation without any role for T cells.
runs through butyrate, which works by expanding the regulatory T cells.
would appear in humans carrying K7 just as strongly as it does in mice.
explanation: There are three links: K7 raises butyrate, butyrate expands regulatory T cells, and those cells suppress allergic inflammation. Butyrate alone matches the bacterium's effect, which points to butyrate rather than direct contact. Butyrate fails without regulatory T cells, which shows that it acts through them. Only this choice keeps every link.

A.why: You kept the T cells but went back to the 'direct action' view the passage undercuts. Butyrate alone reproduces the effect, which points away from the bacterium binding to the cells.

B.why: You stopped at the first link, butyrate. The last finding shows butyrate does nothing without regulatory T cells, so the T cells are required.

D.why: You carried a finding from mice over to humans. The study was done only in mice.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In great tits, individuals that explore unfamiliar places quickly are also more likely to switch to a new food source when a familiar one runs out. In one suburban population, researchers found that fast exploration was associated with a particular variant of a dopamine-receptor gene, while fast and slow explorers did not differ in body size. Taken together, these findings suggest that in this population, a bird's variant of the gene could help predict ______
choices: its body size as well as how readily it switches to a new food source.
how quickly it explores new places, though not how readily it switches food.
how readily it switches to a new food source when a familiar one runs out.
whether it will survive a winter in which its familiar food source fails.
explanation: The shared term is exploration speed. The gene variant goes with fast exploration, and fast exploration goes with switching food. Remove the middle term and the gene variant goes with food switching. Body size was the variable that stayed the same, so it drops out of the chain.

A.why: You took body size along with the rest. Fast and slow explorers did not differ in size, so the gene gives you nothing to predict size with.

B.why: You used only the first fact. Exploration speed links straight to food switching, so dropping that second step leaves out the very link the passage builds.

D.why: You added one more step, from switching food to surviving. The passage never connects either trait to survival.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: All the stars in a cluster formed at about the same time, and the more massive a star is, the sooner it uses up the hydrogen in its core and leaves the main sequence. So as a cluster ages, stars of lower and lower mass leave the main sequence. Cluster K is roughly twice as old as cluster M. If star P in cluster K is still on the main sequence while star R in cluster M has already left it, then ______
choices: star R is older than star P.
star R is more massive than star P.
star P is more massive than star R.
every star in cluster M is more massive than star P.
explanation: Chain three facts. R has left the main sequence in M, so R is heavier than M's cutoff mass. K is older, so K's cutoff mass is lower than M's. P is still on the main sequence in K, so P is lighter than K's cutoff. Put together: R > M's cutoff > K's cutoff > P.

A.why: You read leaving the main sequence as a sign of age. Stars in a cluster are the same age, and cluster M is the younger one, so R is younger than P.

C.why: You reversed the chain, maybe because P belongs to the older cluster. A star that is still on the main sequence in an older cluster has to be lighter than one that has left it in a younger cluster.

D.why: You stretched one comparison to a whole cluster. Stars still on M's main sequence can be any small mass, so 'every' is not established.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Iron from plant foods is poorly absorbed, but vitamin C eaten in the same meal raises how much of it the body takes up. Tea is often blamed for lowering iron absorption. However, nutrition researcher Priya Raman found that tea's polyphenols reduce absorption of plant iron only when the tea is drunk within an hour of the meal. In her trial, participants ate a lentil meal with orange juice, which is rich in vitamin C, and drank black tea two hours later. Compared with the same meal eaten with water and no tea, their absorption of the lentils' iron would be expected to be ______
choices: about the same, because the tea would cancel the boost from the juice.
lower, because tea polyphenols reduce the absorption of plant iron.
higher, because the tea came too late to offset the juice's boost.
higher, because tea taken after a meal also aids iron absorption.
explanation: The juice supplies vitamin C with the meal, so absorption goes up. The tea's polyphenols matter only within an hour, and this tea came two hours later, so it removes nothing. The net result is higher absorption than the plain meal.

A.why: You saw both effects and let them cancel out. You missed the time limit: tea two hours later is outside the one-hour window, so it offsets nothing.

B.why: You used only the popular view that tea lowers iron absorption. Raman's finding limits that effect to tea taken within an hour, and you also left out the juice.

D.why: You got the direction right but gave a reason nobody stated. The passage says late tea fails to lower absorption, not that it raises it.
